title: Where the Pressure Goes
endLine: With pressure held steady, each tissue's arterioles set its flow.

scenes.tts: Take a thin thigh muscle in an anesthetized cat. Only about fifteen percent of arterial pressure is spent crossing its capillary bed. Yet capillaries are its narrowest vessels. So where does the rest go?
scenes.narration: Take a thin thigh muscle in an anesthetized cat. Only about 15 percent of arterial pressure is spent crossing its capillary bed. Yet capillaries are its narrowest vessels. So where does the rest go?
scenes.caption: Take a thin thigh muscle in an anesthetized cat. Only about 15 percent of arterial pressure is spent crossing its capillary bed. Yet capillaries are its narrowest vessels. So where does the rest go?
scenes.visual: THE WORLD, built here and kept for the whole film (16:9). COLOUR BY CONCEPT, same in every scene: blood pale RED dots; pressure WHITE (bars, gauges, the profile line); arterioles and their smooth-muscle rings ORANGE (the tap); capillaries CYAN; small artery, venule and vein SLATE grey tubes; the muscle bed's flow GOLD; all other beds PURPLE (from s06). LAYOUT: across the upper 60% of the frame, one muscle bed drawn left to right as a single path, filling the frame width: a wide SLATE small artery, a narrower ORANGE arteriole wrapped in ring bands, a fan of about 12 thin CYAN capillaries side by side, merging into a SLATE venule, then a wide SLATE vein leaving at right. Label 'muscle bed' above it. Pale red dots flow left to right all film, slowing as they spread through the capillary fan. Lower 35% of the frame is kept empty for the pressure plot (from s03). Hook motion: a tall WHITE bar at the left edge labelled 'arterial pressure' stands full. As dots cross the capillary fan, a slice of about 15% of the bar's height lights CYAN, labelled 'capillaries: about 15%'; a small tag 'anesthetized cat' sits at top left. On 'narrowest vessels' the capillary fan pulses CYAN. On the question, the remaining 85% of the bar glows WHITE with a large '?', and white text appears across the top: 'Where does the rest go?'
Title 'Where the Pressure Goes' fades in above the path for 2 s while the question text fades out. The WHITE bar at left fades away. Red dots keep flowing through the bed.

scenes.tts: One rule runs everything here. Blood flows from high pressure to low. Through any stretch of vessel, flow equals the pressure drop across it, divided by its resistance.
scenes.narration: One rule runs everything here. Blood flows from high pressure to low. Through any stretch of vessel, flow equals the pressure drop across it, divided by its resistance.
scenes.caption: One rule runs everything here. Blood flows from high pressure to low. Through any stretch of vessel, flow equals the pressure drop across it, divided by its resistance.
scenes.visual: Two WHITE gauges appear: a tall one at the inlet of the small artery labelled 'high', a short one at the outlet of the vein labelled 'low'. On 'high pressure to low', the red dots briefly speed up and a WHITE arrow runs along the path from the high gauge to the low gauge. On 'divided by its resistance', one stretch (the small artery) brightens, and large white text appears above the path, size 34: 'flow = pressure drop ÷ resistance'. It stays at the top through s03, then shrinks to a corner.

scenes.tts: Follow blood through the muscle: a small artery, an arteriole, many capillaries, a venule, a vein. They lie end to end, so the same flow passes every segment. Then each segment's share of the pressure drop equals its share of the resistance.
scenes.narration: Follow blood through the muscle: a small artery, an arteriole, many capillaries, a venule, a vein. They lie end to end, so the same flow passes every segment. Then each segment's share of the pressure drop equals its share of the resistance.
scenes.caption: Follow blood through the muscle: a small artery, an arteriole, many capillaries, a venule, a vein. They lie end to end, so the same flow passes every segment. Then each segment's share of the pressure drop equals its share of the resistance.
scenes.visual: A single highlighted red dot travels the whole path; each segment brightens as the dot enters it and gets its label for a moment ('small artery', 'arteriole', 'capillaries', 'venule', 'vein'); each label fades as the next appears, so no more than two labels show at once. On 'end to end', two small counters appear, one at the inlet and one at the outlet, ticking up at exactly the same rate, with the tag 'same flow'. On 'share of the pressure drop', the empty plot fades in below the path: y axis 'pressure (mmHg)' 0 to 100, x positions lined up with the segment boundaries above, no line drawn yet.

scenes.tts: Here are made-up round numbers, chosen so the capillaries match the cat. Ninety millimeters of mercury drive blood across the bed. The arterioles spend about sixty percent of it. The capillaries spend about fifteen.
scenes.narration: Here are made-up round numbers, chosen so the capillaries match the cat. 90 mmHg drive blood across the bed. The arterioles spend about 60 percent of it. The capillaries spend about 15.
scenes.caption: Here are made-up round numbers, chosen so the capillaries match the cat. 90 mmHg drive blood across the bed. The arterioles spend about 60 percent of it. The capillaries spend about 15.
scenes.visual: Tag 'made-up round numbers' at bottom right of the plot, kept while the plot shows. A WHITE pressure line draws itself left to right in step with the dots above, computed from the lesson's worked problem (driving pressure 90 mmHg, mean arterial 93, right atrial 3; drops: small arteries 9, arterioles 54, capillaries 13.5, venules and veins 13.5): 93 at the artery inlet, 84 at the arteriole inlet, 30 at the capillary inlet, 16.5 at the venule inlet, 3 at the vein outlet. Each fall sits under its own segment. On 'about sixty percent', the steep fall under the arteriole fills ORANGE with a bracket '54 of 90: 60%'. On 'about fifteen', the shallow fall under the capillaries fills CYAN with a bracket '13.5 of 90: 15%'. The arteriole above pulses ORANGE, the capillary fan pulses CYAN.

scenes.tts: Why so little in the capillaries? One capillary resists more than one arteriole. But each is short, and so many lie side by side that together they resist less. In muscle, that is a measured fact, not a law.
scenes.narration: Why so little in the capillaries? One capillary resists more than one arteriole. But each is short, and so many lie side by side that together they resist less. In muscle, that is a measured fact, not a law.
scenes.caption: Why so little in the capillaries? One capillary resists more than one arteriole. But each is short, and so many lie side by side that together they resist less. In muscle, that is a measured fact, not a law.
scenes.visual: The plot dims. Camera pushes in on the arteriole and the capillary fan. Two vertical resistance bars appear beside them, tag 'schematic': on 'one capillary', a single capillary is outlined and its CYAN bar rises taller than the ORANGE 'one arteriole' bar. On 'each is short', the outlined capillary visibly shortens. On 'so many lie side by side', the outlined capillary copies itself again and again into the full fan and beyond, and with each copy the CYAN bar shrinks, ending below the ORANGE bar, now labelled 'all capillaries together'. On 'not a law', a small tag 'in muscle' appears beside the bars. Dots keep flowing through the fan.

scenes.tts: Now pull back. Most organs are fed side by side from the aorta and drain side by side. So each sees nearly the same driving pressure, from aorta to right atrium.
scenes.narration: Now pull back. Most organs are fed side by side from the aorta and drain side by side. So each sees nearly the same driving pressure, from aorta to right atrium.
scenes.caption: Now pull back. Most organs are fed side by side from the aorta and drain side by side. So each sees nearly the same driving pressure, from aorta to right atrium.
scenes.visual: The bars and the plot fade out. Camera pulls back: the muscle bed path shrinks to become the TOP branch of a loop that fills about 70% of frame height. At left a thick SLATE aorta splits into two branches: the top branch is the muscle bed (ORANGE arteriole, CYAN capillary fan, label 'muscle', GOLD tint on its flowing dots) and a bottom branch of the same form tinted PURPLE, labelled 'other beds'. Both rejoin at right into a box labelled 'right atrium'. A tall WHITE gauge sits on the aorta labelled 'mean arterial pressure'; a short WHITE gauge sits on the right atrium. On 'the same driving pressure', two WHITE brackets span gauge to gauge along both branches at once, labelled 'same driving pressure'. At far right, two flow bars appear: GOLD 'muscle flow' and PURPLE 'other beds' (schematic heights). Red dots flow through both branches.

scenes.tts: Here is the one idea. The heart and the reflexes hold mean arterial pressure nearly steady. Each tissue then sets its own flow, by setting the resistance of its own arterioles.
scenes.narration: Here is the one idea. The heart and the reflexes hold mean arterial pressure nearly steady. Each tissue then sets its own flow, by setting the resistance of its own arterioles.
scenes.caption: Here is the one idea. The heart and the reflexes hold mean arterial pressure nearly steady. Each tissue then sets its own flow, by setting the resistance of its own arterioles.
scenes.visual: On 'hold mean arterial pressure nearly steady', a small heart icon pumps at the aorta's left end, and the WHITE aorta gauge trembles slightly but stays level, with a WHITE tag 'held nearly steady'. On 'its own arterioles', the ORANGE arteriole on each branch glows in turn and a small tap-handle icon appears on each one. Text across the top, size 34: 'Each tissue sets its own flow'. Dots keep flowing.

scenes.tts: Arterioles can do this because their walls are rings of smooth muscle. And by Poiseuille's law, resistance goes as one over the radius to the fourth power.
scenes.narration: Arterioles can do this because their walls are rings of smooth muscle. And by Poiseuille's law, resistance goes as one over the radius to the fourth power.
scenes.caption: Arterioles can do this because their walls are rings of smooth muscle. And by Poiseuille's law, resistance goes as one over the radius to the fourth power.
scenes.visual: Camera pushes in on the muscle branch's arteriole until it fills about 60% of frame height, the rest of the loop still visible at the edges. Its ORANGE ring bands contract and relax gently, squeezing the tube a little and letting it go. On 'radius', a WHITE arrow labelled 'r' spans from the tube's centre to its inner wall. On 'fourth power', a label appears beside it, size 34: 'resistance ∝ 1 / r⁴'. The top text from s07 fades out.

scenes.tts: Let the muscle relax its arterioles. It takes more flow, and the body's total resistance falls. What happens to every other bed depends on whether the pressure is held.
scenes.narration: Let the muscle relax its arterioles. It takes more flow, and the body's total resistance falls. What happens to every other bed depends on whether the pressure is held.
scenes.caption: Let the muscle relax its arterioles. It takes more flow, and the body's total resistance falls. What happens to every other bed depends on whether the pressure is held.
scenes.visual: Camera eases back to the whole loop. The ORANGE rings on the muscle arteriole relax and the tube widens; GOLD-tinted dots stream faster through the muscle branch and the GOLD 'muscle flow' bar grows. A WHITE bar labelled 'total resistance' appears at top right and shortens. On 'every other bed', the PURPLE 'other beds' bar dims and gets a '?' (its height not changed or explained), and the 'held nearly steady' tag on the aorta gauge turns into a '?' tag 'held or not?'. Do not show what happens; leave both question marks open.

scenes.tts: But how far must they open? To halve their resistance, how much wider must the arterioles get? Twice as wide? Or much less?
scenes.narration: But how far must they open? To halve their resistance, how much wider must the arterioles get? Twice as wide? Or much less?
scenes.caption: But how far must they open? To halve their resistance, how much wider must the arterioles get? Twice as wide? Or much less?
scenes.visual: The two '?' tags from s09 fade out. Camera pushes back in on the muscle arteriole, now back at its starting width, with the 'r' arrow and 'resistance ∝ 1 / r⁴' label. A WHITE resistance bar beside it shows its current height and a dashed line at half that height labelled 'half'. On 'twice as wide', a dashed ghost outline of the tube at double the radius appears; on 'much less', a second dashed ghost only a little wider appears. Question text at the top in white: 'How much wider halves resistance?'

Predict pause. The question card stays. Near-stillness by design: the two dashed ghosts shimmer faintly, the ORANGE rings breathe slightly, red dots drift slowly through the arteriole. No answer is shown.

scenes.tts: Much less. About nineteen percent wider doubles the radius to the fourth power, so resistance halves. A small change in radius makes a large change in resistance.
scenes.narration: Much less. About 19 percent wider doubles the radius to the fourth power, so resistance halves. A small change in radius makes a large change in resistance.
scenes.caption: Much less. About 19 percent wider doubles the radius to the fourth power, so resistance halves. A small change in radius makes a large change in resistance.
scenes.visual: Question card dissolves. The ORANGE rings relax and the tube widens smoothly until it matches the slightly wider ghost; a readout counts up beside it, computed from resistance ∝ 1 / r⁴: 'r: 1.00 → 1.19', then 'r⁴: 1.0 → 2.0'. In step, the WHITE resistance bar falls to the dashed 'half' line. The double-radius ghost stays faint with the computed label '2× wider: 1/16 resistance', then fades. Dots speed up through the widened tube.

scenes.tts: So in muscle, most of the pressure is spent where the taps are. Hold that pressure steady, and each tissue's own arterioles decide how much blood it gets.
scenes.narration: So in muscle, most of the pressure is spent where the taps are. Hold that pressure steady, and each tissue's own arterioles decide how much blood it gets.
scenes.caption: So in muscle, most of the pressure is spent where the taps are. Hold that pressure steady, and each tissue's own arterioles decide how much blood it gets.
scenes.visual: Pull back to the whole loop; the flow bars and resistance readouts are gone. On 'where the taps are', a faint ghost of the s04 pressure line appears under the muscle branch with its steep ORANGE arteriole fall glowing, then fades. On 'Hold that pressure steady', the WHITE aorta gauge settles with its 'held nearly steady' tag back. On 'each tissue's own arterioles', the tap-handle icons on both branches glow together. Red dots keep flowing through both branches.

End card over the dimmed but still moving loop (red dots flowing through both branches, ORANGE rings breathing gently). Large white text, centred: 'With pressure held steady, each tissue's arterioles set its flow.'
